sections.heading: 8.1 Distance to uncontrollability
sections.text: A classic nearness problem, arising from control theory, concerns pairs of matrices rather than a single one. Definition 8.1 . Let A ∈ ℂ n × n , B ∈ ℂ n × m A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n},B\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m} . The pair ( A , B ) (A,B) is said to be controllable if rank ⁡ ( [ A − λ ​ I B ] ) = n ​ ∀ λ ∈ ℂ . \rank\left(\begin{bmatrix}A-\lambda I&B\end{bmatrix}\right)=n\ \forall\ \lambda\in\mathbb{C}. Since it is clear that the rank condition in Definition 8.1 is always attained for λ ∉ Λ ⁡ ( A ) \lambda\not\in\Lambda(A) , it suffices to check it for at most n n values of λ \lambda , corresponding to the eigenvalues of A A . Uncontrollability means that some left eigenvector of A A is orthogonal to the range of B B . Thus, controllability is a generic property, and robustness of control theory algorithms motivates the computation of the distance of a given matrix pair ( A , B ) (A,B) to the nearest uncontrollable pair, that is, the distance from the nearest matrix pair that does not satisfy Definition 8.1 ; see, for example, Paige (1981) , Wicks and De Carlo (1991) , Gu (2000) , Gu et al. (2006) , Mitchell (2021) and, for an overview, ( Datta 2004 , Chapter 6) . We can reduce to a classic matrix nearness problem by identifying the pair ( A , B ) (A,B) with the matrix [ A B ] ∈ ℂ n × ( m + n ) \displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}A&B\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times(m+n)} . If we then define ℰ unc = { [ X Y ] ∈ ℂ n × ( n + m ) : ∃ λ ∈ ℂ ∣ rank [ X − λ ​ I Y ] < n } , \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{unc}}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}X&Y\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times(n+m)}:\exists\ \lambda\in\mathbb{C}\mid\rank\begin{bmatrix}X-\lambda I&Y\end{bmatrix}<n\right\}, (90) this reduces to a matrix nearness problem in the sense of ( 5 ). Together with Proposition 1.1 , Proposition 8.2 below guarantees the existence of a nearest uncontrollable pair for every input ( A , B ) (A,B) . Proposition 8.2 . Let ℰ unc \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{unc}} be the set defined as in ( 90 ). Then, ℰ unc \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{unc}} is closed. Proof 8.3 . Consider a sequence ( M k ) k ⊂ ℰ unc (M_{k})_{k}\subset\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{unc}} with M k = [ X k Y k ] M_{k}=\begin{bmatrix}X_{k}&Y_{k}\end{bmatrix} , X k ∈ ℂ n × n X_{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n} , Y k ∈ ℂ n × m Y_{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m} , and suppose M k → M = [ X Y ] M_{k}\rightarrow M=\begin{bmatrix}X&Y\end{bmatrix} so that X k → X , Y k → Y X_{k}\rightarrow X,\ Y_{k}\rightarrow Y . Then, for all k k , there exists λ k ∈ ℂ \lambda_{k}\in\mathbb{C} such that [ X k − λ k ​ I Y k ] \begin{bmatrix}X_{k}-\lambda_{k}I&Y_{k}\end{bmatrix} does not have full row rank. Noting that λ k \lambda_{k} must be an eigenvalue of X k X_{k} , following the same argument as in the proof of Proposition 4.1 we can construct a convergent subsequence ( λ k j ) j → λ ∈ ℂ (\lambda_{k_{j}})_{j}\rightarrow\lambda\in\mathbb{C} . By the lower semicontinuity of the rank, it then follows that rank ⁡ ( [ X − λ ​ I Y ] ) ≤ lim inf j → ∞ rank ⁡ ( [ X k j − λ k j ​ I Y k j ] ) < n ⇒ M ∈ ℰ unc . \rank\left(\begin{bmatrix}X-\lambda I&Y\end{bmatrix}\right)\leq\liminf_{j\rightarrow\infty}\rank\left(\begin{bmatrix}X_{k_{j}}-\lambda_{k_{j}}I&Y_{k_{j}}\end{bmatrix}\right)<n\Rightarrow M\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{unc}}. The same reasoning that led to ( 32 ) yields a two-level formulation also for the distance to uncontrollability problem, with the inner problem solved by the Schmidt-Eckart-Young-Mirsky Theorem (Example 3.14 ). To state Theorem 8.4 , which was first proved by Eising (1984) let us begin by denoting the distance to uncontrollability of the pair ( A , B ) (A,B) as τ ⁡ ( A , B ) = min [ A + Δ ​ A B + Δ ​ B ] ∈ ℰ unc ⁡ ‖ [ Δ ​ A Δ ​ B ] ‖ . \tau(A,B)=\min_{\scriptsize\begin{bmatrix}A+\Delta A&B+\Delta B\end{bmatrix}\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{unc}}}\left\|\begin{bmatrix}\Delta A&\Delta B\end{bmatrix}\right\|. (91) Theorem 8.4 . Let A ∈ ℂ n × n A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n} and B ∈ ℂ n × m B\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times m} , and specialize ( 91 ) to an arbitrary unitarily invariant norm ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| such that ‖ e 1 ​ e 1 T ‖ = 1 \|e_{1}e_{1}^{T}\|=1 . Then, denoting by σ k ​ ( M ) \sigma_{k}(M) the k k -th singular value of the matrix M M , it holds τ ⁡ ( A , B ) = min λ ∈ ℂ ⁡ σ n ​ ( [ A − λ ​ I B ] ) . \tau(A,B)=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}}\sigma_{n}\left(\begin{bmatrix}A-\lambda I&B\end{bmatrix}\right). (92) Moreover, if λ 0 \lambda_{0} attains the minimum in ( 92 ) and u u (resp. v v ) is a left (resp. right) singular vector of [ A − λ 0 ​ I B ] \begin{bmatrix}A-\lambda_{0}I&B\end{bmatrix} associated with the singular value σ n \sigma_{n} , then the rank-one perturbation [ Δ A Δ B ] = − σ n ​ u ​ v ∗ \begin{bmatrix}\Delta_{A}&\Delta_{B}\end{bmatrix}=-\sigma_{n}uv^{*} , partitioned conformably, is a global minimizer. Proof 8.5 . Arguing as in the proof of Theorem 4.8 , τ ⁡ ( A , B ) \displaystyle\tau(A,B) = min λ ∈ ℂ ⁡ min ⁡ { ‖ [ Δ A Δ B ] ‖ : rank ⁡ ( [ A − λ ​ I + Δ A B + Δ B ] ) < n } \displaystyle=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}}\,\min\left\{\left\|{\begin{bmatrix}\Delta_{A}&\Delta_{B}\end{bmatrix}}\right\|:\rank\left(\begin{bmatrix}A-\lambda I+\Delta_{A}&B+\Delta_{B}\end{bmatrix}\right)<n\right\} = min λ ∈ ℂ ⁡ σ n ​ ( [ A − λ ​ I B ] ) , \displaystyle=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}}\sigma_{n}\left(\begin{bmatrix}A-\lambda I&B\end{bmatrix}\right), where the inner minimum and the form of the minimizer directly follow from Example 3.14 applied to the matrix [ A − λ ​ I B ] \begin{bmatrix}A-\lambda I&B\end{bmatrix} . Equation ( 92 ) is only superficially similar to ( 31 ). However, an important difference is that the minimization is now over the whole complex plane, as opposed to the boundary ∂ Ω \partial\Omega . This reveals a higher complexity. Indeed, at least for a sufficiently regular target set Ω \Omega , one can hope to parametrize its boundary by one real variable; on the other hand, the eigenvalue at which controllability is lost can lie anywhere in ℂ \mathbb{C} , and therefore σ n ​ ( λ ) \sigma_{n}(\lambda) in ( 92 ) must be minimized as a function of the two real variables ℜ ⁡ ( λ ) \Re(\lambda) and ℑ ⁡ ( λ ) \Im(\lambda) . Observe also that, by Weyl’s inequalities, for all | λ | > ∥ A ∥ 2 + ∥ B ∥ 2 |\lambda|>\lVert A\rVert_{2}+\lVert B\rVert_{2} it holds σ n ​ ( λ ) 2 = λ min ​ ( ( A − λ ​ I n ) ​ ( A − λ ​ I n ) ∗ + B ​ B ∗ ) ≥ σ n ​ ( A − λ ​ I n ) 2 ≥ ( | λ | − ∥ A ∥ 2 ) 2 > ∥ B ∥ 2 2 . \sigma_{n}(\lambda)^{2}=\lambda_{\min}\left((A-\lambda I_{n})(A-\lambda I_{n})^{*}+BB^{*}\right)\geq\sigma_{n}(A-\lambda I_{n})^{2}\geq(\lvert\lambda\rvert-\lVert A\rVert_{2})^{2}>\lVert B\rVert_{2}^{2}. Since the perturbation [ Δ A Δ B ] = [ 0 − B ] \displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}\Delta_{A}&\Delta_{B}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-B\end{bmatrix} shows that τ ⁡ ( A , B ) = min λ ∈ ℂ ⁡ σ n ​ ( λ ) ≤ ∥ B ∥ 2 \tau(A,B)=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}}\sigma_{n}(\lambda)\leq\lVert B\rVert_{2} (recalling that we assume a normalization of the unitarily invariant norm via ‖ e 1 ​ e 1 T ‖ = 1 \|e_{1}e_{1}^{T}\|=1 , by Theorem 8.4 , there is no loss of generality in using the spectral norm), we conclude that the minimum in ( 92 ) is attained in the compact set | λ | ≤ ∥ A ∥ 2 + ∥ B ∥ 2 |\lambda|\leq\lVert A\rVert_{2}+\lVert B\rVert_{2} . However, the real function σ n ​ ( ℜ ⁡ λ , ℑ ⁡ λ ) \sigma_{n}(\Re\lambda,\Im\lambda) is not generally convex nor smooth, and may possess many local minima; moreover, no analogue of the Hamiltonian eigenvalue test of Theorem 4.13 is known that certifies global optimality via a single structured eigenvalue computation. Local optimization methods for ( 92 ) were analyzed in Wicks and De Carlo (1991) . Gu (2000) proposed a test that, given δ > 0 \delta>0 , verifies at least one of the two inequalities τ ⁡ ( A , B ) ≤ δ \tau(A,B)\leq\delta and τ ⁡ ( A , B ) > δ / 2 \tau(A,B)>\delta/2 ; Gu’s test is based on a very large structured eigenvalue problem. When enhanced with a bisection scheme, this yields an estimate of τ ⁡ ( A , B ) \tau(A,B) within a factor of 2 2 in polynomial time; a trisection variant that computes τ ⁡ ( A , B ) \tau(A,B) to arbitrary accuracy was proposed in Burke et al. (2004) . The dominant cost of the verification step, a dense eigenvalue problem of dimension O ⁡ ( n 2 ) O(n^{2}) , was later reduced by Gu et al. (2006) using shift-and-invert iterations, bringing the complexity down to O ⁡ ( n 4 ) O(n^{4}) on average and O ⁡ ( n 5 ) O(n^{5}) in the worst case. More recently, Mitchell (2021) proposed interpolation-based globality certificates , which, assuming sufficiently accurate interpolation, certify a posteriori that a candidate local minimizer of ( 92 ) is global, and which perform well in practice also on larger problems. Earlier algorithms for computing Kreiss constants, based on large eigenvalue problems, were developed in Mitchell (2020) . Several variations on this theme have been studied. If A A and B B are real and the perturbations are constrained to be real, one obtains the real distance to uncontrollability, which can be strictly larger than ( 91 ) and is related to real structured singular values; see Qiu et al. (1995) . The discussion above transfers verbatim to the distance to unobservability, by simply taking transpose conjugates of all the involved n × ( m + n ) n\times(m+n) matrices.

Another classic in numerical linear algebra is Wilkinson’s problem , which consists in finding the nearest defective matrix, i.e., the nearest matrix that has non-semisimple eigenvalues. Note that the set of defective matrices is not closed: For instance, [ a ε 0 a ]  egin{bmatrix}a&\varepsilon\ 0&a\end{bmatrix} is defective for ε ≠ 0 \varepsilon
eq 0 , but for ε = 0 \varepsilon=0 it has merely a double eigenvalue. The closure of the set 𝒟 \mathcal{D} of defective matrices is precisely 𝒟 ¯ = { X : X has repeated (i.e., non-distinct) eigenvalues } ; \overline{\mathcal{D}}=\{X\colon	ext{$X$ has repeated (i.e., non-distinct) eigenvalues}\}; To ensure that the distance problem d ⁡ ( A , 𝒟 ) d(A,\mathcal{D}) has a minimum rather than an infimum, we would need to replace it with d ⁡ ( A , 𝒟 ¯ ) d(A,\overline{\mathcal{D}}) , as discussed in Section 1.1 . However, we shall see in the following that, for every A ∈ 𝔽 n × n A\in\mathbb{F}^{n	imes n} with n n simple distinct eigenvalues, there are minimizers in 𝒟 \mathcal{D} for every unitarily invariant norm, and in particular for the Frobenius norm all such minimizers are in 𝒟 . \mathcal{D}. u-1 , but this is not generally true for every other unitarily invariant norm. Indeed, for example, in the spectral norm 0 0 is a nearest singular matrix to the identity. The distance to the nearest defective matrix is related to the conditioning of the eigenvalue and eigenvector problems, since 𝒟 \mathcal{D} is precisely the set for which they are ill-posed. This motivated the initial interest on this problem by Wilkinson and Demmel Wilkinson (1972) , Wilkinson (1984) , Demmel (1987) . Lemma 8.6 gives a useful equivalent condition to check when X ∈ 𝒟 ¯ X\in\overline{\mathcal{D}} that is used by several algorithms. The result is folklore; for a proof, see for instance Kalinina et al. (2023) . Lemma 8.6 . An eigenvalue λ \lambda of a matrix X ∈ ℂ n × n X\in\mathbb{C}^{n	imes n} is non-simple (multiple and/or defective) if and only if there exist a left eigenvector u u and a right eigenvector v v which are orthogonal, i.e., v ∗ ​ u = 0 v^{*}u=0 . Malyshev (1999) gives an algebraic characterization for the solution of Wilkinson’s problem. Theorem 8.7 ( Malyshev (1999) ) . Let A ∈ ℂ n × n A\in\mathbb{C}^{n	imes n} . Define ℰ 0 , 0 = { X ∈ ℂ n × n : X has a repeated eigenvalue 0 } \mathcal{E}_{0,0}=\{X\in\mathbb{C}^{n	imes n}\colon	ext{$X$ has a repeated eigenvalue $0$}\} (so that every matrix in ℰ 0 , 0 \mathcal{E}_{0,0} has either a multiple semisimple eigenvalue in 0 0 , or at least one nilpotent Jordan block of size at least 2 2 ). Then, in the distance induced by the spectral norm ∥ ⋅ ∥ 2 \lVert\cdotVert_{2} , d ⁡ ( A , ℰ 0 , 0 ) = max γ ≥ 0 ⁡ σ 2 ​ n − 1 ​ ( M ⁡ ( A , γ ) ) , where ​ M ​ ( A , γ ) = [ A γ ​ I n 0 A ] . d(A,\mathcal{E}_{0,0})=\max_{\gamma\geq 0}\sigma_{2n-1}(M(A,\gamma)),\quad	ext{where }M(A,\gamma)= egin{bmatrix}A&\gamma I_{n}\ 0&A\end{bmatrix}. (93) In particular, this implies that d ⁡ ( A , 𝒟 ¯ ) = min λ ∈ ℂ ⁡ d ⁡ ( A − λ ​ I n , ℰ 0 , 0 ) = min λ ∈ ℂ ⁡ max γ ≥ 0 ​ σ 2 ​ n − 1 ​ ( M ⁡ ( A − λ ​ I n , γ ) ) . d(A,\overline{\mathcal{D}})=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}}d(A-\lambda I_{n},\mathcal{E}_{0,0})=\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{C}}\max_{\gamma\geq 0}\sigma_{2n-1}(M(A-\lambda I_{n},\gamma)). (94) Proof 8.8 . (Sketch) Proving the inequality d ⁡ ( A , ℰ 0 , 0 ) ≥ max γ ≥ 0 ⁡ σ 2 ​ n − 1 ​ ( M ⁡ ( A , γ ) ) d(A,\mathcal{E}_{0,0})\geq\max_{\gamma\geq 0}\sigma_{2n-1}(M(A,\gamma)) in Theorem 8.7 is easy: If A − Δ A-\Delta has a double eigenvalue 0 0 or a nilpotent Jordan block in 0 0 , then for any given γ \gamma we can use the eigenvectors or the Jordan chain to construct two linearly independent vectors inside ker ⁡ M ⁡ ( A − Δ , γ ) \ker M(A-\Delta,\gamma) . Hence M ⁡ ( A − Δ , γ ) M(A-\Delta,\gamma) has rank at most 2 ​ n − 2 2n-2 , and ∥ Δ ∥ 2 \displaystyle\lVert\DeltaVert_{2} = ∥ M ⁡ ( A − Δ , γ ) − M ⁡ ( A , γ ) ∥ 2 ≥ d ⁡ ( M ⁡ ( A , γ ) , ℛ ≤ 2 ​ n − 2 ) = σ 2 ​ n − 1 ​ ( M ⁡ ( A , γ ) ) . \displaystyle=\lVert M(A-\Delta,\gamma)-M(A,\gamma)Vert_{2}\geq d(M(A,\gamma),\mathcal{R}_{\leq 2n-2})=\sigma_{2n-1}(M(A,\gamma)). The converse inequality is significantly more involved, and a constructive proof requires explicitly finding a matrix Δ \Delta satisfying both A − Δ ∈ ℰ 0 , 0 A-\Delta\in\mathcal{E}_{0,0} and ∥ Δ ∥ 2 = max γ ≥ 0 ⁡ σ 2 ​ n − 1 ​ ( M ⁡ ( A , γ ) ) \lVert\DeltaVert_{2}=\max_{\gamma\geq 0}\sigma_{2n-1}(M(A,\gamma)) . The construction in Malyshev (1999) splits into several subcases, distinguishing whether γ = 0 \gamma=0 or not in the maximum, and whether σ 2 ​ n − 1 ​ ( M ⁡ ( A , γ ) ) = σ 2 ​ n ​ ( M ⁡ ( A , γ ) ) \sigma_{2n-1}(M(A,\gamma))=\sigma_{2n}(M(A,\gamma)) . We have not been able to find a less technical argument, and so we do not include a proof here. We may replace the domain γ ≥ 0 \gamma\geq 0 with γ ∈ ℝ \gamma\in\mathbb{R} with no loss of generality in the statement of Theorem 8.7 , because replacing γ \gamma with − γ -\gamma does not alter the singular values. Note the similarity of ( 93 ) with formulas such as ( 31 ) for the distance to instability. Using a language due to Alam (2023) , we may generalize both. Let C ∈ ℂ k × k C\in\mathbb{C}^{k	imes k} be given, with k ≤ n k\leq n , and define ℰ ∼ C = { X ∈ ℂ n × n : X = V ​ [ C ∗ 0 ∗ ] ​ V − 1 ​ for some nonsingular V ∈ ℂ n × n } , \mathcal{E}_{\sim C}=\left\{X\in\mathbb{C}^{n	imes n}\colon X=V egin{bmatrix}C&*\ 0&*\end{bmatrix}V^{-1}	ext{ for some nonsingular $V\in\mathbb{C}^{n	imes n}$}ight\}, where ∗ * denotes a block whose exact nature is not relevant. In other words, ℰ ∼ C \mathcal{E}_{\sim C} is the set of matrices similar to a block triangular matrix having C C in its upper left corner. Every X ∈ ℰ ∼ C X\in\mathcal{E}_{\sim C} has the same eigenvalues as C C , counted with multiplicities, plus others. One has Alam (2023) d ⁡ ( A , ℰ ∼ C ) ≥ σ n ​ k − k + 1 ​ ( I k ⊗ A − C ⊤ ⊗ I n ) . d(A,\mathcal{E}_{\sim C})\geq\sigma_{nk-k+1}(I_{k}\otimes A-C^{	op}\otimes I_{n}). so maximizing over one or more parameters γ i \gamma_{i} appearing in C C one can obtain bounds for d ⁡ ( A , ℰ ∼ C ) d(A,\mathcal{E}_{\sim C}) . Unfortunately, in general this bound is only an inequality: A certain rank assumption on the singular vectors must hold in the general case to construct a matrix at that exact distance. Malyshev’s result is recovered with C = [ 0 0 γ 0 ] C= egin{bmatrix}0&0\ \gamma&0\end{bmatrix} ; Gracia (2005) , Lippert (2005) studied in more detail the case of a matrix with two distinct eigenvalues C = [ λ 1 0 γ λ 2 ] C= egin{bmatrix}\lambda_{1}&0\ \gamma&\lambda_{2}\end{bmatrix} , and Mengi (2011) the case of a multiplicity higher than 2. A more appealing geometric characterization of the solution of Wilkinson’s problem based on pseudospectra is due to Lippert and Edelman (1999) (in the regular case) and Alam and Bora (2005) (in the general case). To describe it, we start from some observations on the pseudospectra of a matrix A ∈ ℂ n × n A\in\mathbb{C}^{n	imes n} with distinct eigenvalues. First-order eigenvalue perturbation theory tells us that for small ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 the pseudospectrum Λ ε ​ ( A ) \Lambda_{\varepsilon}(A) is composed of n n disjoint connected components ℛ 1 , ε , … , ℛ n , ε \mathcal{R}_{1,\varepsilon},\dots,\mathcal{R}_{n,\varepsilon} each resembling (to first order) a small disk of radius κ ⁡ ( A , λ j ) ​ ε \kappa(A,\lambda_{j})\varepsilon centered in an eigenvalue λ j \lambda_{j} of A A . No additional connected components can appear as we increase ε \varepsilon : Otherwise, ∥ ( A − z ​ I n ) − 1 ∥ 2 = max ∥ x ∥ 2 = ∥ y ∥ 2 = 1 ⁡ | x ∗ ​ ( A − z ​ I n ) − 1 ​ y | \lVert(A-zI_{n})^{-1}Vert_{2}=\max_{\lVert xVert_{2}=\lVert yVert_{2}=1}\lvert x^{*}(A-zI_{n})^{-1}yvert would have a local maximum outside Λ ⁡ ( A ) \Lambda(A) , and this would violate the maximum modulus principle, since it is a maximum of absolute values of holomorphic functions in z z . So, as we increase ε \varepsilon , these n n components become larger, and eventually they touch and merge. We call the smallest ε \varepsilon for which Λ ε ​ ( A ) \Lambda_{\varepsilon}(A) has fewer than n n connected components the first coalescence level , and denote it by ε ⋆ \varepsilon_{\star} . A point where the closures of two distinct connected components of the open pseudospectrum { z : σ min ​ ( A − z ​ I n ) < ε ⋆ } \{z:\sigma_{\min}(A-zI_{n})<\varepsilon_{\star}\} meet is called a first coalescence point z ⋆ z_{\star} . (2011) prove that ε ⋆ = d ⁡ ( A , 𝒟 ) \varepsilon_{\star}=d(A,\mathcal{D}) , in each unitarily invariant norm (recall that the pseudospectra coincide for all such norms, up to normalization by a multiplicative constant). The key result to prove this equality is the following. Theorem 8.9 ( Alam et al. (2011, Theorem 5) ) . Let A ∈ ℂ n × n A\in\mathbb{C}^{n	imes n} have distinct eigenvalues. If z ⋆ z_{\star} is a first coalescence point of the pseudospectrum Λ ε ⋆ ​ ( A ) \Lambda_{\varepsilon_{\star}}(A) , then there exist a pair of singular vectors u ⋆ , v ⋆ ∈ ℂ n u_{\star},v_{\star}\in\mathbb{C}^{n} associated to ε ⋆ = σ n ​ ( A − z ⋆ ​ I n ) \varepsilon_{\star}=\sigma_{n}(A-z_{\star}I_{n}) such that v ⋆ ∗ ​ u ⋆ = 0 v_{\star}^{*}u_{\star}=0 . Proof 8.10 . (Sketch.) The proof is easier when the smallest singular value σ n ​ ( A − z ⋆ ​ I n ) \sigma_{n}(A-z_{\star}I_{n}) is simple. In this case, let u , v u,v be the associated singular vectors (unique up to a phase). The reader might be tempted to see the case of a repeated singular value as an uninteresting non-generic complication, but we note that it actually arises in cases of practical relevance for applications. For example, it always happens when A A is normal; see Example 8.17 below. But first, we conclude the geometric characterization of d ⁡ ( A , 𝒟 ) d(A,\mathcal{D}) . Theorem 8.11 . sections.heading: 8.3 Stratifications
8.4 Miscellanea
sections.text: The line of research of matrix nearness problems is vast, and includes some topics that do not fit well in the categories that we have treated in the previous sections. We conclude our discussion of matrix problems (before having a look at what happens beyond matrices) with a few examples of nearness problems having a different character.

sections.heading: 8.4.1 Reversible Markov chains.
sections.text: Given a transition matrix P P and a prescribed positive probability vector π \pi , one can seek a nearby stochastic matrix satisfying various constraints: min X ∈ ℝ n × n ⁡ ‖ X − P ‖ F 2 s.t. X ​ 𝟏 = 𝟏 , X ≥ 0 , D π ​ X = X T ​ D π , D π = diagm ⁡ ( π ) . \min_{X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}}\|X-P\|_{F}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad X\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},\quad X\geq 0,\quad D_{\pi}X=X^{T}D_{\pi},\qquad D_{\pi}=\diagm(\pi). Here the inequality is elementwise, and reducible matrices are allowed. Nielsen and Weber (2015) reformulate this task as a convex optimization problem. Durastante et al. (2026a) develop a Riemannian approach using the Fisher metric, while Cipolla et al. (2026) study a quadratic programming formulation with sparsity constraints. A related problem aims at a reduction in Kemeny’s constant, which measures an average hitting time, while simultaneously minimizing the size of the perturbation. Durastante et al. (2026b) study this double-objective problem.

sections.heading: 8.4.2 Stabilization with nonnegative entries
sections.text: A natural structured variant of the nearest weakly Schur stable matrix problem is min { ∥ X − A ∥ : X ≥ 0 , ρ ( X ) ≤ 1 } , \min\{\|X-A\|:X\geq 0,\ \rho(X)\leq 1\}, where A ≥ 0 A\geq 0 and ρ \rho denotes the spectral radius. Although the feasible set is nonconvex, Nesterov and Protasov (2020) obtain global solution methods for the max norm (provably in polynomial time), and the induced matrix 1 1 - and ∞ \infty -norms. Their approach is based on properties of the Perron eigenvalue.

sections.heading: 8.4.3 Matrix compressions
sections.text: An application to atomic physics motivates the nearness problem min Y ∈ ℝ n × p , Y T ​ Y = I p ⁡ ‖ Y T ​ N ​ Y − T ‖ F 2 , \min_{Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p},\,Y^{T}Y=I_{p}}\|Y^{T}NY-T\|_{F}^{2}, where N ≥ 0 N\geq 0 is a given symmetric positive definite matrix and T T is diagonal. Borsdorf (2014) construct an optimal solution and study related problems using Riemannian geometry and an augmented Lagrangian method.

sections.heading: 8.4.4 Parameter optimization
sections.text: Some instances of nearness problems can involve a family of matrices depending on just a few parameters, say, A ⁡ ( θ ) A(\theta) , where the optimization only involves the vector θ ∈ ℝ m \theta\in\mathbb{R}^{m} . For example, Mengi (2018) develop various optimization methods to maximize the distance from instability for matrices depending on a few parameters; these algorithms come with convergence guarantees.

sections.heading: 9 Beyond matrices
sections.text: A common generalization of ( 5 ) consists of replacing 𝔽 m × n \mathbb{F}^{m\times n} by the vector space of polynomial matrices of degree at most k k , and taking ℰ \mathcal{E} to be a closed subset of this vector space. (Arguably, the case of highest interest in practice is that of pencils , where k = 1 k=1 .) These are polynomials with matrix coefficients, P ⁡ ( z ) = A 0 + A 1 ​ z + ⋯ + A k ​ z k , A i ∈ 𝔽 m × n ​ ∀ 0 ≤ i ≤ k . P(z)=A_{0}+A_{1}z+\dots+A_{k}z^{k},\quad A_{i}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times n}\ \forall\ 0\leq i\leq k. If we consider the norm ‖ P ⁡ ( z ) ‖ F := ∑ i = 0 k ‖ A i ‖ F 2 , \|P(z)\|_{F}:=\sqrt{\sum_{i=0}^{k}\|A_{i}\|_{F}^{2}}, (98) it is clear once again that Theorem 1.6 and Corollary 1.8 apply because this metric vector space is isomorphic to 𝔽 ( k + 1 ) ​ m ​ n \mathbb{F}^{(k+1)mn} equipped with the Frobenius distance. Hence, with the distance induced by ( 98 ), it also makes sense to pose the nearness problem ( 5 ) for matrix pencils, or generally polynomial matrices, thus going beyond single matrices. Other objects on which nearness problems have appeared include state-space realizations of transfer functions or tensors. It is undeniable that these topics are close neighbors of matrix nearness problems but, to avoid an incontrollable growth of this survey’s length, we will not discuss them at the same level of detail as we did for matrices. Instead, in this section we only provide a brief, and necessarily partial, overview of selected results in these adjacent areas.

sections.heading: 9.1 Distance from singularity
sections.text: Let us start with the case of polynomial matrices P ⁡ ( z ) = ∑ i = 0 k A i ​ z i P(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}A_{i}z^{i} . Recall Noferini (2024) that a square polynomial matrix P ⁡ ( z ) P(z) is called singular if det P ⁡ ( z ) \det P(z) is the zero polynomial, and regular otherwise. Possibly, the simplest possible extension to polynomials of the class of spectrally constrained nearness problems is to require that P ⁡ ( z ) P(z) becomes singular at a prescribed point λ ∈ ℂ \lambda\in\mathbb{C} ; for a regular polynomial, this is tantamount to asking that λ \lambda is a finite eigenvalue (whereas, if the input is singular, then the distance is 0 0 and the problem is trivial). This problem admits a closed-form solution, that we describe in Proposition 9.1 , whose proof follows a topos in polynomial eigenvalue perturbation theory; see, e.g., Tisseur (2000, Theorem 5) or Nakatsukasa et al. (2015, Theorem 1) . For a connection with pseudospectral theory, see Tisseur and Higham (2001) . Proposition 9.1 . Let P ⁡ ( z ) = ∑ i = 0 k A i ​ z i P(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}A_{i}z^{i} with A i ∈ ℂ n × n A_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n} for i = 0 , … , k i=0,\dots,k . The squared distance of P ⁡ ( z ) P(z) from the set of polynomial matrices that are singular at λ \lambda , measured in the distance induced by the Frobenius norm ( 98 ), is given by ‖ Δ ⁡ ( z ) ‖ F 2 = σ min 2 ​ ( P ⁡ ( λ ) ) η ⁡ ( λ ) , \|\Delta(z)\|_{F}^{2}=\frac{\sigma_{\min}^{2}(P(\lambda))}{\eta(\lambda)}, where σ min ​ ( X ) \sigma_{\min}(X) denotes the smallest singular value of the matrix X X and η ⁡ ( λ ) := ∑ j = 0 k | λ | 2 ​ j \eta(\lambda):=\sum_{j=0}^{k}|\lambda|^{2j} . Proof 9.2 . Let Δ ⁡ ( z ) = ∑ i = 0 k E i ​ z i \Delta(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}E_{i}z^{i} be such that P ⁡ ( λ ) + Δ ⁡ ( λ ) P(\lambda)+\Delta(\lambda) is singular. Then, using the Schmidt-Eckart-Young-Mirsky Theorem (Example 3.14 ) and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, σ min ​ ( P ⁡ ( λ ) ) ≤ ‖ Δ ⁡ ( λ ) ‖ F ≤ η ⁡ ( λ ) ⋅ ‖ Δ ⁡ ( z ) ‖ F . \sigma_{\min}(P(\lambda))\leq\|\Delta(\lambda)\|_{F}\leq\sqrt{\eta(\lambda)}\cdot\|\Delta(z)\|_{F}. Hence, there cannot be a Δ ⁡ ( z ) \Delta(z) having smaller norm. It remains to find a polynomial having precisely that norm; to this goal, let u , v u,v be unit left and right singular vectors of P ⁡ ( λ ) P(\lambda) associated with σ := σ min ​ ( P ⁡ ( λ ) ) \sigma:=\sigma_{\min}(P(\lambda)) , and take E i := − σ ​ ( λ ¯ ) i η ⁡ ( λ ) u v ∗ , i = 0 , … , k . E_{i}:=-\frac{\sigma(\overline{\lambda})^{i}}{\eta(\lambda)}uv^{*},\quad i=0,\dots,k. In contrast with the simple Proposition 9.1 , the structured variant of this problem, for example when a linear constraint is imposed on the coefficients of Δ ⁡ ( z ) \Delta(z) , already grows in complexity Tisseur and Higham (2001) . The prescription of one eigenvalue can be made more demanding by moving in at least two different directions. Fixing not just one but several eigenvalues, Kressner et al. (2014) study the distance in the spectral norm from a given pencil to pencils with (partially) prescribed spectrum, by only perturbing the trailing matrix coefficient. Under suitable assumptions, they characterize the distance by optimizing singular values; the analogous problem for higher-degree polynomial matrices is studied by Karow and Mengi (2015) . Or one can prescribe an elementary divisor and not just an eigenvalue. Das and Bora (2020) study the distance to matrix polynomials having an elementary divisor ( z − λ ) j (z-\lambda)^{j} with j ≥ r j\geq r , for prescribed λ ∈ ℂ \lambda\in\mathbb{C} and 2 ≤ r ≤ n ​ k 2\leq r\leq nk . For regular polynomials, this requires a Jordan chain of length at least r r at λ \lambda . They characterize the distance through structured low-rank approximation of a block Toeplitz matrix built from derivatives of the polynomial at λ \lambda , obtaining both optimization algorithms and exact bounds. A stronger requirement is to make the polynomial matrix singular, so that its determinant vanishes at all points. If the maximal degree of a perturbed polynomial matrix P ⁡ ( z ) − Δ ⁡ ( z ) P(z)-\Delta(z) is fixed, then the subset of singular polynomial matrices is closed and therefore a least norm perturbation Δ ⁡ ( z ) \Delta(z) that makes P ⁡ ( z ) − Δ ⁡ ( z ) P(z)-\Delta(z) singular exists. For pencils, the problem of finding the distance to singularity is studied by Byers et al. (1998) , who give several characterizations and bounds. The ODE-based method of Guglielmi et al. (2017) is applicable both to finding the nearest singular pencil and to finding the nearest pencil having a constant vector in its kernel (right minimal index zero). The two problems are not the same, because for a pencil A 0 + A 1 ​ z A_{0}+A_{1}z to be singular the existence of a shared vector in the null spaces of A 0 A_{0} and A 1 A_{1} is a sufficient, but not necessary condition. This is illustrated by the example ker ⁡ ( [ 1 − z 0 0 0 − z 0 0 1 ] ) = span ⁡ ( [ z 1 0 ] ) . \ker\left(\begin{bmatrix}1&-z&0\\ 0&0&-z\\ 0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\right)=\spann\left(\begin{bmatrix}z\\ 1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}\right). Generally, the least possible degrees in a polynomial basis for the null space of a polynomial matrix are called minimal indices ; see Forney Jr. (1975) , Noferini (2024) and the references therein. A method for the nearest singular pencil based on Riemannian optimization over unitary matrices is proposed by Dopico et al. (2024) . Every pair of matrices can be brought to triangular form by unitary equivalence, that is, T 0 = Q ​ A 0 ​ Z , T 1 = Q ​ A 1 ​ Z T_{0}=QA_{0}Z,T_{1}=QA_{1}Z for upper triangular T 0 , T 1 T_{0},T_{1} and unitary Q , Z ∈ U ⁡ ( n ) Q,Z\in U(n) . On the other hand, an upper triangular pencil is singular if and only if at least one of its diagonal elements is zero. Hence, a pencil version of ( 38 ) can be written, leading to the optimization over ( Q , Z ) ∈ U ⁡ ( n ) × U ⁡ ( n ) (Q,Z)\in U(n)\times U(n) of the objective function f ⁡ ( Q , Z ) = ∑ i > j ( | ( Q ​ A 0 ​ Z ) i ​ j | 2 + | ( Q ​ A 1 ​ Z ) i ​ j | 2 ) + min 1 ≤ k ≤ n ⁡ ( | ( Q ​ A 0 ​ Z ) k ​ k | 2 + | ( Q ​ A 1 ​ Z ) k ​ k | 2 ) . f(Q,Z)=\sum_{i>j}\left(|(QA_{0}Z)_{ij}|^{2}+|(QA_{1}Z)_{ij}|^{2}\right)+\min_{1\leq k\leq n}\left(|(QA_{0}Z)_{kk}|^{2}+|(QA_{1}Z)_{kk}|^{2}\right). In Dopico et al. (2024) , various algorithms to minimize f ⁡ ( Q , Z ) f(Q,Z) are proposed, including smooth alternatives and variants involving prescribed minimal indices. For higher-degree polynomials, a useful connection with structured low-rank approximation comes from polynomial null vectors. If v ⁡ ( λ ) = ∑ j = 0 ℓ λ j ​ v j v(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}\lambda^{j}v_{j} , then P ( λ ) v ( λ ) ≡ 0 ⇔ ∑ i + j = r 0 ≤ i ≤ k 0 ≤ j ≤ ℓ A i v j = 0 , r = 0 , … , k + ℓ . P(\lambda)v(\lambda)\equiv 0\Leftrightarrow\quad\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j=r\\ 0\leq i\leq k\\ 0\leq j\leq\ell\end{subarray}}A_{i}v_{j}=0,\quad r=0,\ldots,k+\ell. These equations form a block Toeplitz linear system in the coefficients { v j } j = 0 ℓ \{v_{j}\}_{j=0}^{\ell} . Both Das and Bora (2023) and Gnazzo et al. (2026b) start from these block Toeplitz convolutions to characterize distances and derive optimization formulations and bounds; the resulting algorithms are however different, with Das and Bora (2023) exploiting Euclidean optimization and ad hoc formulae and Gnazzo et al. (2026b) adopting Riemannian optimization and Tikhonov regularization. An alternative approach is to enforce singularity at sufficiently many evaluation points. Since deg det P ≤ n k \deg\det P\leq nk , a degree- k k n × n n\times n polynomial P P is singular if and only if P ⁡ ( λ i ) P(\lambda_{i}) is singular at n ​ k + 1 nk+1 distinct evaluation points { λ i } i = 0 n ​ k \{\lambda_{i}\}_{i=0}^{nk} . This approach is developed by Gnazzo and Guglielmi (2025a) , who design an algorithm based on sampling the smallest singular value at sufficiently many evaluation points and driving these values to zero through a structured gradient flow. Adding extra structure can sometimes make these problems more tractable. One example arises when studying dissipative Hamiltonian pencils, for which Mehl et al. (2021) obtain explicit characterizations of the structured distance to singularity. Dmytryshyn et al. (2026) consider instead the distance to the nearest skew-symmetric polynomial matrix of prescribed normal rank, and tackle it numerically by exploiting a rank-revealing factorization.

sections.heading: 9.2 Approximate polynomial GCD
sections.text: A notable application of the structured distance to singularity problem ( 65 ) is the approximate polynomial GCD. The problem is as follows: Given a pair of homogeneous bivariate scalar polynomials p ^ ​ ( x , z ) , q ^ ​ ( x , z ) \hat{p}(x,z),\hat{q}(x,z) (of degrees d p , d q d_{p},d_{q} ), find the nearest pair of polynomials p ⁡ ( x , z ) , q ⁡ ( x , z ) p(x,z),q(x,z) that have a greatest common divisor (GCD) of degree at least d d . The distance between pairs of polynomials here is measured using the distance induced by the 2-norm of their coefficients ∥ ( p , q ) ∥ 2 = ∥ p ∥ 2 + ∥ q ∥ 2 = ∑ j = 0 d p | p j | 2 + ∑ j = 0 d q | q j | 2 \lVert(p,q)\rVert^{2}=\lVert p\rVert^{2}+\lVert q\rVert^{2}=\sum_{j=0}^{d_{p}}\lvert p_{j}\rvert^{2}+\sum_{j=0}^{d_{q}}\lvert q_{j}\rvert^{2} It can be shown that two homogeneous polynomials p ⁡ ( x , z ) , q ⁡ ( x , z ) p(x,z),q(x,z) (of degrees d p , d q d_{p},d_{q} ) have a homogeneous GCD of degree at least d d if and only if the Sylvester matrix S ⁡ ( p , q ) = [ p 0 q 0 p 1 p 0 ⋮ ⋱ ⋮ p 1 ⋱ q d q ⋱ ⋱ p d p ⋮ ⋱ p 0 ⋱ ⋱ ⋱ p d p ⋱ p 1 ⋱ ⋱ q 0 ⋱ ⋮ ⋱ ⋮ p d p q d q ] S(p,q)=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc|ccccc}p_{0}&&&&q_{0}\\ p_{1}&p_{0}&&&\vdots&\ddots\\ \vdots&p_{1}&\ddots&&q_{d_{q}}&\ddots&\ddots\\ p_{d_{p}}&\vdots&\ddots&p_{0}&&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots\\ &p_{d_{p}}&\ddots&p_{1}&&&\ddots&\ddots&q_{0}\\ &&\ddots&\vdots&&&&\ddots&\vdots\\ &&&p_{d_{p}}&&&&&q_{d_{q}}\end{array}\right] (99) (where the two blocks have d q − d + 1 d_{q}-d+1 and d p − d + 1 d_{p}-d+1 columns, respectively) has a right kernel. Note that ∥ S ⁡ ( p , q ) ∥ F 2 = ( d q − d + 1 ) ​ ∥ p ∥ 2 + ( d p − d + 1 ) ​ ∥ q ∥ 2 \lVert S(p,q)\rVert_{F}^{2}=(d_{q}-d+1)\lVert p\rVert^{2}+(d_{p}-d+1)\lVert q\rVert^{2} , hence one needs to rescale suitably the polynomials in S ⁡ ( p , q ) S(p,q) so that the target norms of the two problems agree; but once we do that, the approximate GCD problem can be converted into a structured distance from singularity problem: min ⁡ ∥ ( p − p ^ , q − q ^ ) ∥ 2 ​ s.t. ​ p , q have a GCD of degree at least d = d ​ ( S ⁡ ( 1 d q − d + 1 ​ p ^ , 1 d p − d + 1 ​ q ^ ) , ℰ 0 ∩ 𝒱 ) 2 , \min\lVert(p-\hat{p},q-\hat{q})\rVert^{2}\ \text{s.t.}\ \text{$p,q$ have a GCD of degree at least $d$}\\ =d\left(S\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{q}-d+1}}\hat{p},\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{p}-d+1}}\hat{q}\right),\,\mathcal{E}_{0}\cap\mathcal{V}\right)^{2}, (100) where 𝒱 \mathcal{V} is the space of matrices S ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) S(\cdot,\cdot) with the structure ( 99 ). Remark 9.3 . One can dehomogenize the involved polynomials, recasting the problem as one about univariate polynomials; indeed, this is the most common formulation in the literature. However, in this setting the “if and only if” characterization discussed above no longer holds, due to the possibility of a shared root at infinity. Consider for example the dehomogenized pair p ^ = 2 + x \hat{p}=2+x and q ^ = 2 − x \hat{q}=2-x . Then the input Sylvester matrix is [ 2 2 1 − 1 ] \begin{bmatrix}2&2\\ 1&-1\end{bmatrix} , and its (unique) nearest singular Sylvester matrix in the Frobenius norm is [ 2 2 0 0 ] \begin{bmatrix}2&2\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix} . The latter matrix corresponds to p = q = 2 p=q=2 , whose GCD has degree 0 0 and not 1 1 . The issue here is that the homogenized analogues of the output polynomials are p ⁡ ( x , z ) = q ⁡ ( x , z ) = 2 ​ z p(x,z)=q(x,z)=2z , that share the projective root ( x , z ) = ( 1 , 0 ) (x,z)=(1,0) , and this root blows up to infinity in the affine line. The formulation based on the Sylvester matrix plays also a key role in the structured total least norm algorithms of Kaltofen et al. (2007) . Specialized algorithms from polynomial algebra exist for this problem, so it is a good test bench to assess the effectiveness of the algorithms that we have discussed in Section 6 ; see also Nagasaka (2021) for a comparison of algorithms for approximate polynomial GCDs. Usevich and Markovsky (2017) and Gnazzo et al. (2026b) test SLRA methods on ( 100 ), and conclude that unfortunately these methods may have accuracy issues when d 2 ​ ( A , ℰ 0 ∩ ( A + 𝒱 ) ) d^{2}(A,\mathcal{E}_{0}\cap(A+\mathcal{V})) becomes the order of machine precision or smaller; possibly this is due to the conditioning of the problem reformulation with the Sylvester matrix ( 99 ). Two more effective methods for this problem that do not use ( 99 ) appear also in Usevich and Markovsky (2017) with the names V ​ P h VP_{h} and V ​ P g VP_{g} : They still rely on variable projection ideas, but they are no longer based on solving a matrix distance problem. Fazzi et al. (2019) use a variant of the methods that we described in Section 7.2 , with target function F ​ ( A ) = σ min ​ ( A ) F(A)=\sigma_{\min}(A) . The authors compare to SLRA, and the experiments display the fact that SLRA without the regularization technique in ( 75 ) may miss the global minimum and converge to a worse local one.

sections.heading: 9.3 Stability, hyperbolicity, and more
sections.text: The eigenvalues of a regular matrix pencil A 0 + z ​ A 1 A_{0}+zA_{1} are usually defined on the Riemann sphere; an infinite eigenvalue corresponds to a zero eigenvalue of the reversed pencil A 1 + z ​ A 0 A_{1}+zA_{0} . If we fix a nonempty closed subset Ω \Omega of the Riemann sphere, the set of the regular pencils with all eigenvalues in Ω \Omega is not closed, but one can still compute the distance to this set as well as a nearest pencil in the closure. A Riemannian optimization approach, based on optimization over U ⁡ ( n ) × U ⁡ ( n ) U(n)\times U(n) is developed by Noferini and Nyman (2025) . This method is again based on a variant of ( 38 ), with the inner minimization solved based on projective projections of pairs of complex numbers. Related nearness problems for stable descriptor systems are studied by Gillis et al. (2018) for Hurwitz stability and by Gillis et al. (2020) for Schur stability, the latter with further rank constraints. Other distance problems arise in the context of Hermitian polynomial matrices. For example, a quadratic polynomial matrix P ⁡ ( z ) = A 0 + A 1 ​ z + A 2 ​ z 2 P(z)=A_{0}+A_{1}z+A_{2}z^{2} Tisseur and Meerbergen (2001) with A 2 ≻ 0 A_{2}\succ 0 is called hyperbolic if x ∗ ​ P ​ ( z ) ​ x x^{*}P(z)x has two distinct real roots for every nonzero vector x x . Hyperbolicity is equivalent to the inequality ( x ∗ ​ A 1 ​ x ) 2 − 4 ​ ( x ∗ ​ A 0 ​ x ) ​ ( x ∗ ​ A 2 ​ x ) > 0 ∀ x ≠ 0 . (x^{*}A_{1}x)^{2}-4(x^{*}A_{0}x)(x^{*}A_{2}x)>0\quad\forall\ x\neq 0. Analogously, a Hermitian quadratic polynomial matrix with A 2 ≻ 0 A_{2}\succ 0 is called elliptic if ( x ∗ ​ A 1 ​ x ) 2 − 4 ​ ( x ∗ ​ A 0 ​ x ) ​ ( x ∗ ​ A 2 ​ x ) < 0 (x^{*}A_{1}x)^{2}-4(x^{*}A_{0}x)(x^{*}A_{2}x)<0 for every nonzero vector x x . Higham et al. (2002) study the distance from a hyperbolic quadratic polynomial to one outside the class, together with related problems for definite Hermitian pairs and elliptic quadratic polynomials. Hachez and Van Dooren (2003) prove more related results, both on the distance to non-hyperbolic and non-elliptic Hermitian polynomials and also on the two reverse nearness problems (distance to hyperbolic polynomials and distance to elliptic polynomials). State-space realizations provide a further example of a nearness problem. The transfer function of a continuous time realization ( A , B , C , D ) (A,B,C,D) is defined as the rational matrix G ⁡ ( s ) = C ​ ( s ​ I − A ) − 1 ​ B + D . G(s)=C(sI-A)^{-1}B+D. In applications, a property called bounded-realness requires that G G is analytic on the closed right half-plane and satisfies G ​ ( i ​ ω ) ∗ ​ G ​ ( i ​ ω ) ⪯ I G(i\omega)^{*}G(i\omega)\preceq I for every ω ∈ ℝ \omega\in\mathbb{R} . Cherifi et al. (2025) study the distance to bounded-real systems via port-Hamiltonian representations and numerical optimization.

sections.heading: 9.4 Matrix-valued functions and tensors
sections.text: To extend nearness problems beyond polynomial matrices, we can replace the monomials { z j } j = 0 k \{z^{j}\}_{j=0}^{k} with a finite set { f j ​ ( z ) } j = 0 k \{f_{j}(z)\}_{j=0}^{k} of linearly independent entire functions. Thus, a polynomial matrix P ⁡ ( z ) P(z) is replaced by an analytic matrix-valued function F ⁡ ( z ) = ∑ j = 0 k A j ​ f j ​ ( z ) F(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}A_{j}f_{j}(z) , and perturbations take the form Δ ⁡ ( z ) = ∑ j = 0 k E j ​ f j ​ ( z ) \Delta(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}E_{j}f_{j}(z) . The norm ( 98 ) extends trivially to this setup. One example of an application comes from time-delay equations, where F ⁡ ( z ) F(z) takes the form z ​ I − A 0 − e − τ ​ z ​ A 1 zI-A_{0}-e^{-\tau z}A_{1} . Gnazzo and Guglielmi (2025b) develop an approximation method, based on analytic approximation, to compute the distance to singular matrix-valued functions ( det F ⁡ ( z ) ≡ 0 \det F(z)\equiv 0 ), including the case where the coefficient matrices of the perturbation Δ ⁡ ( z ) \Delta(z) must satisfy further linear constraints. A different variation on this theme is studied by Karow et al. (2014) , who look for a constant matrix E E of least spectral norm such that F ⁡ ( z ) + E F(z)+E has prescribed eigenvalues with prescribed algebraic multiplicities. Finally, the boldest numerical linear algebraist might dare make the leap from matrices to tensors. Tensor nearness problems provide an extension in which even existence of a best low-rank approximation can fail. The CP rank of a tensor is the least number of elementary tensor products needed to express it as a sum. For order three, the set of tensors of CP rank at most two need not be closed ( de Silva and Lim 2008 ) . For instance, let e 1 , e 2 e_{1},e_{2} be the vectors in the canonical basis of ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} and write v ⊗ 3 = v ⊗ v ⊗ v v^{\otimes 3}=v\otimes v\otimes v . Then, consider the sequence ( W k ) k ≥ 1 (W_{k})_{k\geq 1} such that W k = k ⁡ ( ( e 1 + 1 k ​ e 2 ) ⊗ 3 − e 1 ⊗ 3 ) ⟶ W = e 2 ⊗ e 1 ⊗ e 1 + e 1 ⊗ e 2 ⊗ e 1 + e 1 ⊗ e 1 ⊗ e 2 . W_{k}=k\left((e_{1}+\tfrac{1}{k}e_{2})^{\otimes 3}-e_{1}^{\otimes 3}\right)\longrightarrow W=e_{2}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{1}+e_{1}\otimes e_{2}\otimes e_{1}+e_{1}\otimes e_{1}\otimes e_{2}. For all k ≥ 1 k\geq 1 , W k W_{k} has CP rank at most 2 2 , but its limit W W has CP rank 3 3 . Therefore, the distance from W W to the set of tensors of CP rank at most 2 2 is zero (and there is no nearest such tensor). This behavior is of course very different from that of matrices. To further complicate matters, different notions of tensor rank exist, leading to different results about the existence, or lack thereof, of low-rank tensor approximations. For example, the multilinear rank of a tensor of order 3 3 is the triple of matrix ranks obtained by flattening the tensor in three different ways (isolating one index at a time against the other two). In high contrast with the CP rank, a nearest (in the Euclidean distance) tensor always exists among those whose multilinear rank is elementwise bounded above by a triple ( r 1 , r 2 , r 3 ) (r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}) . For further related notions, we refer to Kolda and Bader (2009) for a survey of tensor decompositions and algorithms.

sections.heading: 10 Conclusions
sections.text: Matrix nearness problems combine a simple formulation with a rich variety of theoretical and computational challenges. In this review, we have emphasized a few aspects in particular, such as the geometry of the feasible set, the choice of the distance, and the effect of imposing additional structure on admissible perturbations. We have also examined the interplay between the properties of these problems and the features of the algorithms used to solve them. Among the (in our opinion) most useful ideas that we hope to have illustrated are matrix decompositions as a source of useful parametrizations, variable projection as a way to reduce dimensionality, and the use of geometric tools such as normal spaces and orthogonal projections. We have also pointed out several subtleties, particularly concerning existence, regularity, and the distinction between local and global optimality. Along the way, we have also filled a few gaps in the literature (see page 1 ), and we are especially proud of this outcome. Even before starting this review, we knew that the literature on matrix nearness problems was vast, but only while exploring did we realize how many interesting papers we had not encountered before. Unlike mathematics itself, mathematical papers must unfortunately be finite, and therefore we have had to be selective. We apologize to colleagues whose relevant contributions to nearness problems we have overlooked or have been unable to include. We hope that the mathematical and algorithmic connections presented here will provide a useful guide for future research on matrix nearness problems. We had a lot of fun exploring the literature and writing this article, and we hope that our readers will share some of that enjoyment.

University of Pisa Largo Pontecorvo 3 56127 Pisa Italy E-mail: federico.poloni@unipi.it Abstract Given a nonempty set of matrices ℰ ⊆ ℂ m × n \mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{m	imes n} and a matrix A ∉ ℰ A
ot\in\mathcal{E} , a matrix nearness problem (or matrix distance problem) consists in finding a matrix in ℰ \mathcal{E} that is closest to A A , in some norm, as well as the corresponding distance. This article is a survey of matrix nearness problems and of numerical algorithms for their solution. We pay special attention to modern related topics, such as Riemannian optimization and pseudospectra, that were not discussed in depth in previous reviews about this topic. Besides collecting known facts, we also prove some foundational results that, at least in the present form, we could not locate in the literature. 1 Introduction A matrix nearness problem can be described very simply: We are given a matrix A A and a nonempty closed set ℰ \mathcal{E} , often described as the locus of a property which is not enjoyed by A A . Can we find a matrix X ⋆ ∈ ℰ X_{\star}\in\mathcal{E} nearest to A A ? If not, can we at least compute, or bound effectively, the distance from ℰ \mathcal{E} to A A ? Such problems arise naturally across a range of fields. In some matrix nearness problems ( Higham 2002 , e.g.,) , the input matrix A A is supposed to have the desired property that characterizes the set ℰ \mathcal{E} , but in reality it does not because errors of various nature (modelling, measurement, numerical approximation…) have been made in forming A A , and one seeks to correct these errors. On other occasions ( Van Loan 1985 , e.g.,) the property is on the contrary unwanted: The target set ℰ \mathcal{E} contains matrices associated with ill-posedness of a class of problems (linear systems, generalized eigenvalue problems, differential equations…), and thus the distance from it can be used as a proxy for the robustness of the instance of the problem associated with the input A A . This interpretation connects matrix nearness problems with the study of conditioning via the distance to ill-posedness Bürgisser and Cucker (2013) , Demmel (1987) , Rump (1999) . This viewpoint is not completely uncontroversial; Trefethen (2007) discusses further subtleties, focusing in particular on structured perturbations. There are many concrete applications of matrix nearness problems. We collect but a few illustrative examples in the non-exhaustive list below. • Control theory: nearest stable matrix Higham (1989) , Gillis and Sharma (2017) , Guglielmi and Protasov (2018) , Noferini and Poloni (2021) or nearest unstable matrix Van Loan (1985) , Byers (1988) , Kressner (2006) , Gnazzo et al. (2026b) , Guglielmi and Lubich (2026) ; • Finance: nearest correlation matrix Higham (2002) ; • Numerical algebraic geometry: approximate GCD Bini and Boito (2010) , Zeng (2011) , Usevich and Markovsky (2017) , Gnazzo et al. (2026b) ; • Numerical linear algebra: low-rank approximation Schmidt (1907) , Eckart and Young (1936) , Mirsky (1960) , distance to defective matrices Malyshev (1999) , Alam et al. (2011) , or topics closely related to nearness problems such as matrix completion Keshavan et al. (2010) , Vandereycken (2013) ; • Quantum information theory: nearest unitary gate or density matrix Nielsen and Chuang (2010) ; • Signal processing and machine learning: nearest unitary matrix Higham (1986) or improving the robustness of neural ODEs De Marinis et al. (2025) . From both the analytic and the numerical perspective, the difficulty of a matrix nearness problem is highly dependent on the choice of the target set ℰ \mathcal{E} , as well as on the choice of the bivariate function used to measure distances between matrices. The dependence on ℰ \mathcal{E} is clear: • Certain problems admit a closed-form solution, say, the Hermitian matrix nearest to A A in the Frobenius distance is its Hermitian part 1 2 ​ ( A + A ∗ )  rac{1}{2}(A+A^{*}) Fan and Hoffman (1955) , Higham (1989) ; • Others can be solved by very robust algorithms, say, the nearest matrix of rank ≤ 1 \leq 1 in the Frobenius distance can be easily computed via the Singular Value Decomposition (henceforth abbreviated SVD Schmidt (1907) , Eckart and Young (1936) , Mirsky (1960) ); • Some more are provably difficult: For example, even deciding whether an affine subspace of real matrices contains a singular matrix is NP-hard Zhang et al. (2023) ; • And many more have been explored only marginally, if at all: For example, how do we find the matrix nearest to a given one and having a prescribed numerical range? The choice of the distance can also dramatically influence the hardness of the problem. The Euclidean (Frobenius) distance combines two nice properties: It is unitarily invariant, and it leads to a convenient Hilbert space setting. Arguably, these features make the Frobenius distance the most comfortable choice mathematically, but applications sometimes call for other choices, the most common of which are perhaps the distances induced by the spectral norm or other unitarily invariant norms. We are not the first to review theoretical results and numerical algorithms related to matrix nearness problems. In particular, we would like to acknowledge one source of inspiration from the beginning. Starting very early on in his career, Higham (1985) , Higham (1986) , Higham (1988) studied matrix nearness problems, and already in 1989 he wrote a highly influential survey Higham (1989) that identified the most crucial and essential mathematical aspects for this class of problems, with his characteristic clarity and elegance. Our aim is not to replace Higham’s review, but to complement it. To ensure self-containedness, we will inevitably have to overlap somewhat with the material in Higham (1989) ; however, we regard our paper as a natural sequel. We therefore focus primarily on developments that have taken place in the last four decades, and on advanced analytic and algorithmic aspects that were not treated in the earlier survey. We shall explore this subject along two dimensions: numerical methods for matrix nearness problems, and representative classes of problems to which these methods apply. Our treatment is (perhaps necessarily, to keep the length reasonable) selective, with particular emphasis on the geometry of nearest-matrix projections, spectral constraints, and structured perturbations. A recurring theme that we have tried to emphasize throughout our review is how these viewpoints lead to useful reformulations and numerical algorithms. This editorial choice had some painful side effects, and we had to leave some important areas outside the scope of our detailed treatment; notably, among other topics, matrix completion ( Wright and Ma 2022 , Section 4.4) and nonnegative matrix factorization Gillis (2020) . The topic of matrix nearness problems ramifies into fairly many branches of mathematics, and to keep our treatment concise we will sometimes assume without justification basic results that can be found in textbooks such as (for example): Horn and Johnson (1991) , Horn and Johnson (2013) , Hogben (2014) for matrix theory, Trefethen and Bau III (1997) , Golub and Van Loan (2013) for numerical linear algebra, Petersen (2016) , Lee (2018) for differential geometry, Rockafellar (1970) , Hiriart-Urruty and Lemaréchal (1993) for convex analysis, Rudin (1976) , Rudin (1991) for mathematical analysis, or Boumal (2023) , Nocedal and Wright (2006) for optimization. As can be expected for a survey article, we have mostly collected results that have previously appeared elsewhere. Nonetheless, when a concise and instructive proof of a known result can be given, we have done so for the sake of self-containedness; our proofs are usually original and may sometimes depart significantly from the classic ones. The article also includes results that, at least in the form given here, we have not been able to easily locate in the literature. These novelties include: • Several characterizations of which nearness problems admit a common minimizer for every distance induced by a unitarily invariant norm. Theorem 2.23 analyzes the general case and Theorem 3.12 focuses on unitarily invariant sets; moreover, when the target set is a real affine subspace, we also obtain further equivalent conditions (Theorem 2.25 and Theorem 2.34 ). Some auxiliary results that we developed to this goal, such as items (ii)-(iii) in Lemma 2.30 or Proposition 2.32 , may also be new. • Theorem 2.5 , which shows that, under some differentiability assumptions of the chosen norm, the rank deficient matrix nearest to an input of full rank has rank drop precisely 1 1 ; and Corollary 8.15 , which under the same hypotheses on the norm analogously proves that any matrix with multiple eigenvalues and nearest to one with simple eigenvalues is defective. • Theorem 4.20 , which describes global and local optimality criteria for reformulations of matrix nearness problems as optimization tasks over unitary matrices; on the same theme, Proposition 4.23 extends the corresponding gradient formula beyond what already exists in the literature. • Theorem 6.3 , which is a description of the properties of optimal perturbations when further linear constraints are added to a nearness problem, obtained via the theory of normal cones. This theorem also allows us to extend and generalize a recent result by Guglielmi and Lubich (2026) for the structured distance to singularity (Corollary 6.5 ). • Several examples that we developed to highlight specific phenomena or clarify the limitations of theoretical results; among others in this category, we may mention Example 2.27 , the counterexample within Remark 2.37 , Example 4.22 , Example 4.27 , Example 6.11 , and Example 8.17 . The structure of our review paper is the following. We first continue this introduction with an overview of basic properties of distance functions, nearest points, and normal cones, as well as a more formal definition of matrix nearness problems. In Section 2 we discuss the choice of the distance, paying particular attention to unitarily invariant norms and to the question of whether a matrix nearness problem admits a solution that simultaneously minimizes the distances induced by all these norms. In Section 3 we discuss nearness problems that can be solved directly; our definition of “direct methods” is broad and includes those that exploit a classic matrix decomposition of the input, e.g., the SVD. We then turn our attention to spectral nearness problems in Section 4 , discussing their connections with pseudospectra and with numerical methods based on singular value optimization, optimization over the manifold of unitary matrices, and gradient systems. In Section 5 we describe alternating projection methods for distances to intersections of sets. In the next two sections we study the additional complications (or, occasionally, simplifications) that arise when an extra constraint is added to a nearness problem, focusing on distance to singularity (Section 6 ) and on spectral nearness (Section 7 ). In Section 8 we cover further matrix nearness problems beyond the previous classes, including distance to uncontrollability and distance to matrices with multiple eigenvalues. Finally, in Section 9 , we briefly consider the extension of nearness problems from matrices to matrix pencils, polynomial matrices, matrix-valued functions, and tensors. We conclude the article by offering some final remarks in Section 10 . 1.1 Distance from sets We begin by giving a general overview of the analytic properties of distance functions to a set.
